doc.title: Jackie Williams interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, October 18, 1995

title: Rhythm and blues groups: Johnny Guitar Saunders and Eugene Smith
summary: Before jazz he played R&B and entertainment groups, touring with Johnny Guitar Saunders and Eugene Smith, and met Alan Dawson, Mae Arnett and Jaki Byard in Boston.

story.theme_name: First paying gigs: getting started as a young professional
story.community_name: First paid gigs: pay, bands and young beginnings

blocks.x: What kind of, have you done any non-jazz kind of work? Done any rhythm & blues, that type of thing?

Oh, sure, sure. I did many of those. Prior to getting into more jazz, I used to do quite a bit of what we call Rhythm & Blues and entertainment type group things. They were a lot of fun you know, and very beneficial to your growth also because you get a feeling of entertainment, which all music is, you know. And no matter how serious it is, it’s still supposed to be entertaining. I remember playing with a group, Johnny “Guitar” Saunders, he was a guitar player naturally, and he had a nice entertainment type group. He used to do a lot of things like “Night Train” and stuff, you know those things in the day were very popular. “Night Train” and “Honky Tonk” and stuff like that. But those things were joyful to play. You know the people really liked that. We used to go to a lot of different places. We used to play up in your area — up in Buffalo, Buffalo, New York and Rochester. They had a lot of that kind of stuff in Pennsylvania. We used to go out there

and play the Pueblo Club. And I played with that group a lot for a while. Then I played with another wonderful trio, Eugene Smith. He was very entertaining. He would do a lot of piano, stand up and play the piano and sing and do stuff like that. You know like Maurice Rocco, but Maurice Rocco used to dance. He was a tremendous dancer. And he would dance and play the piano. “Boogie Woogie” and everything. Eugene is very good like that. And he used to idolize Dorothy Donegan because she was such a great performer. And he was very fond of Dorothy’s playing. But Gene was a natural entertainer, as well as he played wonderful piano, but he was more of an entertainer. So I used to do a lot of work with him. And we played a lot of the clubs in New England and some in Canada in the Ontario area, and we used to do a lot of travel. Boston. We went to Boston and we played Wally’s, a place called Wally’s where all of the, most of the jazz players would come and play. And that’s when I was at Wally’s, that’s when I first, with Eugene Smith, I first met Alan Dawson, the great drummer from New England. And I met Mae Arnett. She was a wonderful, great singer. And I met them there — and then Jaki Byard in Boston at that time. And he was playing — you know Jaki plays alto saxophone. And he came and he was playing alto sax. And I said well, “This guy plays so great” but I didn’t know it — he played piano. But when I first met him, you know, that’s all he — but you know as time went on we worked together, not too long ago we worked together, I realized that he was a great piano player. So in all these travels, in different settings, you hook up with so many different things. And they’re all like a puzzle, they all come together. That’s the beauty of music.
